title: Ovarian (adnexal) torsion
subtitle: Suspect it, scope it, untwist it

sources.org: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG)
sources.title: Adnexal torsion in adolescents (Committee Opinion No. 783)

sources.org: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG)
sources.title: Management of suspected ovarian masses in premenopausal women (Green-top Guideline No. 62)

red_flags.text: Sudden-onset unilateral lower abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting, in a girl or woman with a known or found adnexal mass.
Intermittent pain over days that becomes constant: partial torsion that has completed.
Pregnancy, ovarian stimulation for assisted conception, and a mass in a child: all raise the risk.
Fever, peritonism and a raised lactate late in the history: possible necrosis.

do_now.text: Pregnancy test, analgesia, nil by mouth and intravenous access.
Clinical suspicion of torsion is the indication for prompt surgical exploration. Do not wait for a definitive imaging diagnosis.
Call the gynaecologist (or paediatric surgeon for a child) at the point of suspicion, and book theatre.

assess.text: Character and timing of pain, previous episodes, menstrual history, known cysts, fertility treatment.
Abdominal examination for a mass and peritonism; consider appendicitis, ectopic, ruptured cyst and pelvic inflammatory disease.
Haemodynamic status: a haemorrhagic cyst or an ectopic can coexist or mimic.

investigate.text: Pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal where appropriate, transabdominal in children): an enlarged ovary, often with a mass, peripheral follicles or a whirlpool sign of the pedicle.
Normal Doppler flow does not exclude torsion. Dual blood supply means arterial flow can persist in a twisted ovary.
Full blood count, C-reactive protein, hCG; tumour markers only if malignancy is suspected, sent before theatre so they do not delay it.

resuscitate.text: Adequate analgesia and antiemetics; intravenous fluids while nil by mouth.

definitive.text: Laparoscopy with detorsion and ovarian conservation. A dark, blue-black ovary frequently recovers; its appearance at surgery does not reliably predict viability.
Oophorectomy is rarely required and is reserved for a clearly necrotic, disintegrating ovary or a suspected malignancy in a postmenopausal woman.
Cystectomy at the same operation can be difficult in an oedematous ovary; detorsion alone with interval imaging is acceptable, with a delayed cystectomy if the cyst persists.
Suspicious mass features in a premenopausal woman: manage per the RCOG ovarian mass guidance and involve a gynaecological oncologist before radical surgery.

escalate.text: Paediatric surgeon or paediatric gynaecologist for children; adult gynaecology for adolescents according to local arrangement.
Gynaecological oncology if the mass appears malignant.
Obstetric team when torsion occurs in pregnancy.

notes: Torsion is a clinical diagnosis confirmed at laparoscopy. A normal Doppler has sent many ovaries home to infarct.
Untwist and keep. The black ovary that looks dead at surgery often functions on follow-up imaging.
In a child, think about torsion of a normal ovary and of the opposite side in future: consider oophoropexy in recurrent torsion or a single remaining ovary.
